citation.title: How to use Large Language Models for Text Analysis
citation.venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (cs.CL), University of Amsterdam, ILLC; dated 2023-07-25

question: How can social scientists with limited programming experience use LLMs (ChatGPT/GPT-4 via API) for text analysis such as annotation and classification, and how should the results be validated? Illustrated with measuring populism in political speeches.
data: Illustrative example only: speeches from the Global Populism Database (human-coded levels of populism, CSV plus .txt speech files), analysed with GPT-4 32K. The number of speeches and the period are not stated in the text.
method: Step-by-step guide: (1) API access, (2) load data and fit texts in the context window, (3) prompt engineering (instruction built from existing human coder instructions, output format requested as a number then a short motivation, parsed by splitting on a semicolon), (4) call the LLM at temperature 0.2 in a loop, (5) validate against human codes with Krippendorff's alpha, then inspect disagreements and iterate on prompt and concept.

definitions.definition: The formulation of instructions to LLMs for specific tasks or objectives; the instruction is described as the way a social scientific concept is encoded.
definitions.quote: The instruction to the model can be understood as the way in which a particular social scientiﬁc concept is encoded.

definitions.term: Populism (coding concept used in the example)
definitions.definition: Mudde's definition: an ideology separating society into 'the pure people' versus 'the corrupt elite', with politics as the general will; operationalised in the prompt as people-centrism plus anti-elitism, both required.
definitions.quote: A populist text is characterized by BOTH of the following elements: 1. Peoplecentrism

definitions.definition: A measure of inter-rater agreement that accounts for observed agreement and agreement expected by chance; usable for nominal, ordinal or interval data; ranges 0 to 1.
definitions.quote: The Krippendorﬀ's alpha gives a measure of interrater agreement, and is used to assess the extent to which multiple raters or coders agree

definitions.definition: The range of tokens the model can consider when generating responses; a token is roughly 2/3 of a word.
definitions.quote: the range of "tokens" that the model can consider when generating responses. A token corresponds to roughly 2/3 of a word.

proxies.concept: Level of populism in a political text
proxies.indicator: LLM score on a 0-2 scale plus a brief motivation, from an instruction based on human coder guidelines (people-centrism and anti-elitism).
proxies.quote: [Answer with a number in the 0-2 range, followed by a semi-colon, and then a brief motivation.

proxies.indicator: Krippendorff's alpha between LLM scores and the existing human-coded Global Populism Database scores; examination of the largest disagreements.
proxies.quote: we instead use the existing populism database to validate our data.

findings.claim: In the populism example, the LLM's agreement with the database's human coders was alpha 0.635, even though the LLM was not given the original coders' instructions.
findings.quote: The resulting a Krippendorﬀ's alpha of 0.635.

findings.claim: The original human coders had alpha 0.827 (interval level), but they worked together and resolved disagreements, so the authors expect higher agreement for them than for an independent LLM run.
findings.quote: The human coders of the initial data have a Krippendorﬀ's alpha (interval-level) of 0.827

findings.claim: In one of the largest disagreements (a Berlusconi speech coded 1.0 by humans, 0.0 by the LLM), the author judges the LLM's classification reasonable on manual reading.
findings.quote: it thus seems the LLM may have been reasonable in classifying it as non-populist.

findings.claim: The author states that LLMs can be sensitive to prompt design and that the exact instructions are the key conceptual task of LLM-supported text analysis (stated as a caveat, without own test data).
findings.quote: Formulating the exact instructions for the model should thus be understood as the key conceptual task within LLM-supported text analysis.

findings.claim: The guide cites earlier work (reference 17) as showing LLMs can outperform humans at interpretive annotation; this is reported from a cited study, not tested here.
findings.quote: the models can even outperform humans when it comes to interpretive textual analysis

recommendations.claim: Validate LLM output against other methods, benchmarks, ground truth or expert evaluation; do not trust it unchecked.
recommendations.quote: Careful validation is essential to make sure that the models are measuring what we intend

recommendations.claim: A simple validation route: draw a sample and have human coders classify it, then compare with the model.
recommendations.quote: extract a sample of the data, and have human coders manually classifying the items.

recommendations.claim: Start the prompt from the instructions given to human coders for similar tasks.
recommendations.quote: A good starting point for a prompt is often to look at the instructions given to human coders

recommendations.claim: Make the output parseable by requesting a fixed answer format.
recommendations.quote: Make results parseable: You will need to programmatically parse the output of the model.

recommendations.claim: Develop prompt and concept iteratively, studying disagreements between LLM and coders; human coding is not an unquestioned gold standard.
recommendations.quote: it is recommended to use an iterative process of simultaneous prompt and concept development.

recommendations.claim: Treat the LLM like a student assistant and validate; treat its output like data from human coders, with perspectives and biases, not objectivity.
recommendations.quote: must be treated in similar ways as data from human coders

recommendations.claim: Do not send sensitive or confidential material to the LLM API, and report limitations and biases transparently.
recommendations.quote: The API should therefore never be used with sensitive or conﬁdential material.

recommendations.claim: Use a low temperature for more focused, deterministic output (the example uses 0.2).
recommendations.quote: lower values (e.g., 0.2) make it more focused and deterministic.

recommendations.claim: Split or truncate texts that exceed the context window and reassemble results afterwards.
recommendations.quote: be necessary to split texts into several smaller chunks to be analyzed part by part

limitations.point: LLMs embody biases of their training texts and may fail in unexpected ways; their scope and limits are not fully understood.
limitations.quote: they may fail in unexpected ways on speciﬁc tasks or challenges.

limitations.point: LLMs are slower than traditional NLP classifiers, and very large datasets may need sampling; context window limits text length.
limitations.quote: Datasets that involve millions or tens of millions of datapoints can therefore be prohibitively time-consuming to analyze

limitations.point: The data sent to the API provider is accessible to that provider.
limitations.quote: the platform running the LLM ... will receive access to any data that you send to their API.

limitations.point: The validation is a single run on one task (populism) with one model (GPT-4) and one prompt; alpha 0.635 is described as relatively high but no sample size, repeat runs, or per-class error rates are reported in the text. This is a limit I observed, not stated by the author.
The original coders' instructions were not available, so the LLM prompt differs from the human coding guide; agreement is therefore not a clean test.
limitations.quote: the LLM was not even given the same coding instructions as the original coders.

limitations.point: No test of reproducibility across model versions or repeated runs is reported; the example calls a proprietary model with randomness (temperature 0.2). Observed by the reader, not stated.

Source file mismatch: the id is a SAGE-style DOI (10.4135/9781529683707), but the PDF is the arXiv preprint 2307.13106v1 (not peer reviewed), a 6-page guide with code on GitHub. The DOI is not printed in the PDF. Cited claims should be checked against the published version if one is used.
Text extraction showed no instructions addressed to a reader or AI beyond the how-to steps of the guide itself; none acted on.
Library copy is the arXiv preprint 2307.13106v1 (2023), not the SAGE publication the id names; quotes and pages refer to the preprint.
